headline_marked: Bangladesh Bank [[launches new account for expats]] to boost investment
headline: Bangladesh Bank launches new account for expats to boost investment
summary: The 'Non-Resident Exchangeable Taka Account' allows expatriates to save, invest, and take loans for business or personal use in Bangladesh.
details: Bangladesh Bank has introduced the 'Non-Resident Exchangeable Taka Account' to help expatriates use their earnings more effectively and increase investment in the country.
Under the new rules, expats can open savings, current, or fixed deposit accounts through offshore banking units of scheduled banks using foreign currency sent via banking channels.

Funds in these accounts, including interest or profits, are fully repatriable. They can also be used for local payments, transfers to other non-resident accounts, or foreign direct and portfolio investments.

Offshore banking units can now provide loans in Taka to Type-A industrial enterprises in specialized zones using these deposits. These loans are restricted to approved current expenses like salaries, wages, and utility bills.

Expatriates or their nominees can also use these deposits as collateral to secure loans for personal or business purposes. These funds can be used to purchase residential property for own use or non-repatriable investment.
However, the central bank has explicitly prohibited using these loans for investment in the agriculture, plantation, and housing sectors.
Experts believe this system will deepen the financial mediation of remittance income and create a more structured platform for expatriates to participate in national investment.
caption:
New banking options for expats! Bangladesh Bank introduces a specialized account to make investing and borrowing easier for non-residents.

Bangladesh Bank has introduced the 'Non-Resident Exchangeable Taka Account' to help expatriates use their earnings more effectively and increase investment in the country.

Under the new rules, expats can open savings, current, or fixed deposit accounts through offshore banking units of scheduled banks using foreign currency sent via banking channels.

Funds in these accounts, including interest or profits, are fully repatriable. They can also be used for local payments, transfers to other non-resident accounts, or foreign direct and portfolio investments.

Offshore banking units can now provide loans in Taka to Type-A industrial enterprises in specialized zones using these deposits. These loans are restricted to approved current expenses like salaries, wages, and utility bills.

Expatriates or their nominees can also use these deposits as collateral to secure loans for personal or business purposes. These funds can be used to purchase residential property for own use or non-repatriable investment.

However, the central bank has explicitly prohibited using these loans for investment in the agriculture, plantation, and housing sectors.

Experts believe this system will deepen the financial mediation of remittance income and create a more structured platform for expatriates to participate in national investment.

Source: Prothom Alo, Somoy News
